title: Improper Integrals: Unbounded Integrands and Infinite Limits
quickIdea: When the integrand blows up or a limit is infinite, the integral is defined as a limit; it exists only if that limit is finite, and a finite area can belong to an unbounded function.
remember: Unbounded integrand at an interior point c: split at c and take one-sided limits. The integral exists only if both limits are finite.
Infinite limit: the integral from a to infinity is the limit as b grows of the integral from a to b.

Benchmark: the integral of x^(-p) from 1 to infinity converges exactly when p is greater than 1; the integral of x^(-p) from 0 to 1 converges exactly when p is less than 1. The two conditions are opposite, which is why the interval matters.
An unbounded function can still have a finite area: x^(-1/3) on [-1, 1] is unbounded and discontinuous at 0, yet the area between it and the axis is 3.

The odd-function shortcut is invalid across a singularity: the integral of 1/x from -1 to 1 is not 0, it diverges, because each side has an infinite limit even though the formal antiderivative cancels.
For an area question the integrand is |f|, so an odd unbounded function does not cancel at all: both sides add.

example.prompt: For f(x) = x^(-1/3) on [-1, 1], decide whether f is continuous, whether it is bounded, and whether the area between f and the x-axis is finite and non-zero.
example.work: As x approaches 0 from the right f tends to plus infinity and from the left to minus infinity, so f is not continuous at 0 and not bounded on [-1, 1]. The area is the integral of |x^(-1/3)| from -1 to 1. An antiderivative of x^(-1/3) is (3/2) x^(2/3), so the right piece gives (3/2)(1 - s^(2/3)) as s tends to 0, that is 3/2, and the left piece gives 3/2 as well.
example.answer: Not continuous, not bounded, and the area is 3 - non-zero and finite.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 2015 Set 2 Q.26 asks exactly these three statements about x^(-1/3) and the answer is that the function is unbounded and the area is non-zero and finite. The question exists because candidates assume unbounded means infinite area, or read the area as the signed integral, which would be 0 here.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 2015 Set 2 Q.26: let f(x) = x^(-1/3) and A be the area of the region bounded by f and the x-axis as x varies from -1 to 1. Which are true? I. f is continuous on [-1, 1]. II. f is not bounded on [-1, 1]. III. A is non-zero and finite. (A) II only (B) III only (C) II and III only (D) I, II and III.
variations.why: The one-sided limits at 0 are infinite with opposite signs, so I fails and II holds. The area uses the modulus, and each half contributes 3/2, so A = 3, which is finite and non-zero. The signed integral over [-1, 1] would be 0, which is why statement III is about the area and not the integral.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Does the integral from 0 to 1 of x^(-1/2) dx exist, and what is its value?
variations.why: An antiderivative is 2 sqrt(x), and as the lower limit tends to 0 that tends to 0, so the limit is 2. Here p = 1/2 is less than 1, which is exactly the convergent case for a singularity at 0; the same function on [1, infinity) would diverge.

trap.what: Treating an unbounded integrand as if it were continuous, or using an odd-function cancellation across a singularity.
trap.why: The definition is a limit, and a limit may fail to exist. Cancelling two infinite quantities is not arithmetic that the definite integral permits.
trap.counterexample: The integral of 1/x from -1 to 1 looks like 0 because ln|x| is even, but each side diverges: the integral from 0 to 1 of 1/x is the limit of ln(1) - ln(s) = -ln(s) as s tends to 0, which is infinite. The improper integral diverges, so quoting 0 is wrong.

check.question: For which p does the integral of x^(-p) from 1 to infinity converge?
check.answer: Exactly when p is greater than 1.
check.explanation: For p other than 1 the integral up to b is (b^(1-p) - 1)/(1 - p), which stays finite as b grows only if 1 - p is negative, that is p greater than 1. The case p = 1 gives ln b, which grows without bound. The mirror statement at 0 is p less than 1.
